The decade of the **1980s** in [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world "Western world") cinema saw the return of studio-driven pictures, coming from the filmmaker-driven [New Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hollywood "New Hollywood") era of the 1970s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-1) The period was when the "[high concept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_concept "High concept")" picture was popularized by the likes of producers [Don Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Simpson "Don Simpson") and [Jerry Bruckheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Bruckheimer "Jerry Bruckheimer"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-2) where films were expected to be easily marketable and understandable. Therefore, they had cinematic [plots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plot_(narrative) "Plot (narrative)") that could be summarized in one or two sentences. Since then, this method has become the most utilized formula for modern Hollywood [blockbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster_(entertainment) "Blockbuster (entertainment)"). At the same time in [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") cinema, the [Hong Kong film industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Hong_Kong "Cinema of Hong Kong") entered a boom period that significantly elevated its prominence in the international market.

## Trends

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1980s_in_film&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Trends")]

The cinema of the 1980s covered many subgenres, with hybrids crossing between multiple genres. The course strengthened towards creating ever-larger megahit films, which earned more in their opening weeks than most previous movies due in part to scheduling releases when there were less competition for audience interest.

*   _**[Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action\_films "Action films")**_: In the 1970s, action films usually focused on maverick police officers. However, the genre did not become dominant in Hollywood until the 1980s, when it was promoted by action stars such as [Arnold Schwarzenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger"), [Sylvester Stallone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_Stallone "Sylvester Stallone"), [Chuck Norris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Norris "Chuck Norris"), and [Bruce Willis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Willis "Bruce Willis"). Schwarzenegger built an iconic career out of action classics such as _[The Terminator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Terminator "The Terminator")_ (1984), _[Commando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commando\_(1985\_film) "Commando (1985 film)")_ (1985), and _[Predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predator\_(film) "Predator (film)")_ (1987). Stallone starred in _[First Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First\_Blood "First Blood")_ (1982) about a returning [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") veteran fighting a small town sheriff, as well as its sequels _[Rambo: First Blood Part II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rambo:\_First\_Blood\_Part\_II "Rambo: First Blood Part II")_ and _[Rambo III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rambo\_III "Rambo III")_. Previously seen as a taboo in the 1970s, Vietnam War flicks like [Oliver Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Stone "Oliver Stone")'s _[Platoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platoon\_(film) "Platoon (film)")_ and [Stanley Kubrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick")'s _[Full Metal Jacket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full\_Metal\_Jacket "Full Metal Jacket")_ made the conflict a popular subject in the 1980s. Norris starred in the _[Missing in Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missing\_in\_Action\_(film) "Missing in Action (film)")_ trilogy (1984, 1985, 1988) about a Vietnam veteran going back to rescue [POWs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/POW "POW"). The release of _[Die Hard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Die\_Hard "Die Hard")_ in 1988 was particularly influential on the development of the genre in the subsequent decade. In the film, Willis plays a New York City police detective who inadvertently becomes embroiled in a terrorist take-over of a [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California") office building. Riding the [buddy cop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_cop "Buddy cop") wave that was boosted by the likes of the [_Lethal Weapon_ franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lethal_Weapon_(franchise) "Lethal Weapon (franchise)"), Stallone and [Kurt Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Russell "Kurt Russell")'s _[Tango & Cash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tango\_&\_Cash "Tango & Cash")_ became one of the two last Hollywood films to be released in the 1980s.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-numbers-3) Meanwhile, [Hong Kong action cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_action_cinema "Hong Kong action cinema") was being revolutionized by filmmakers [Jackie Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan "Jackie Chan"), [Tsui Hark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsui_Hark "Tsui Hark"), and [John Woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Woo "John Woo"); garnering increased attention all over the world with the likes of _[Project A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project\_A\_(film) "Project A (film)")_ (1983), _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1985\_film) "Police Story (1985 film)")_ (1985), _[A Better Tomorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Better\_Tomorrow "A Better Tomorrow")_ (1986), and _[The Killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Killer\_(1989\_film) "The Killer (1989 film)")_ (1989). Which featured increasingly complex [martial arts and gunfight choreography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_in_film "Combat in film") with generally unsafe and most often uninsured [stunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stunt "Stunt") work. Blazing the trail for newer types of action movies like the [heroic bloodshed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heroic_bloodshed "Heroic bloodshed") subgenre.
*   _**[Animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animation "Animation")**_: In the 1970s, full-length animated films usually focused on adult fare due to the influence of [Ralph Bakshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Bakshi "Ralph Bakshi") films. However, even though they didn't become popular until the late-1990s and 2000s due to public preference of TV animation, some well-known films were made during the 1980s, especially with [Don Bluth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Bluth "Don Bluth"). After he left [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") in 1979, Bluth formed his first [animation studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_Bluth_Studios "Sullivan Bluth Studios") and produced the moderately-successful _[The Secret of NIMH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Secret\_of\_NIMH "The Secret of NIMH")_ (1982). Bluth later teamed up with [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") to produce _[An American Tail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_American\_Tail "An American Tail")_ (1986) and _[The Land Before Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Land\_Before\_Time\_(film) "The Land Before Time (film)")_ (1988) which both became box-office successes, and proved there was still confidence in animation for theaters. After breaking up with Spielberg, Bluth independently produced _[All Dogs Go To Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All\_Dogs\_Go\_To\_Heaven "All Dogs Go To Heaven")_ (1989). Meanwhile, [the Disney studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Animation_Studios "Walt Disney Animation Studios") was having horrible times and the box-office failure of _[The Black Cauldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Cauldron\_(film) "The Black Cauldron (film)")_ (1985) almost put the studio in jeopardy. However, in later years, the modest success of _[The Great Mouse Detective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Great\_Mouse\_Detective "The Great Mouse Detective")_ (1986), and their collaboration with Spielberg on the live-action/animated film _[Who Framed Roger Rabbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who\_Framed\_Roger\_Rabbit "Who Framed Roger Rabbit")_ (1988) directed by [Robert Zemeckis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Zemeckis "Robert Zemeckis"), which was a critical and box office hit, gave Disney enough confidence in its feature animation division. A year later in the penultimate month of the 1980s, the studio released _[The Little Mermaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Little\_Mermaid\_(1989\_film) "The Little Mermaid (1989 film)")_ (1989), directed by [Ron Clements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Clements "Ron Clements") and [John Musker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Musker "John Musker"), which eventually started an era known as the [Disney Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_Renaissance "Disney Renaissance"). Inspired by the success of 1979's _[The Bugs Bunny/Road Runner Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bugs\_Bunny/Road\_Runner\_Movie "The Bugs Bunny/Road Runner Movie")_, [Looney Tunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looney_Tunes "Looney Tunes") compilation films continued with _[The Looney Looney Looney Bugs Bunny Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Looney\_Looney\_Looney\_Bugs\_Bunny\_Movie "The Looney Looney Looney Bugs Bunny Movie")_ (1981), _[Bugs Bunny's 3rd Movie: 1001 Rabbit Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugs\_Bunny's\_3rd\_Movie:\_1001\_Rabbit\_Tales "Bugs Bunny's 3rd Movie: 1001 Rabbit Tales")_ (1982), _[Daffy Duck's Fantastic Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daffy\_Duck's\_Fantastic\_Island "Daffy Duck's Fantastic Island")_ (1983) and _[Daffy Duck's Quackbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daffy\_Duck's\_Quackbusters "Daffy Duck's Quackbusters")_ (1988). That decade also saw a brief resurgence of popular-toys-based films. [Nelvana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelvana "Nelvana")'s _[The Care Bears Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Care\_Bears\_Movie "The Care Bears Movie")_ (1985) was successful enough to warrant two sequels: _[Care Bears Movie II: A New Generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Care\_Bears\_Movie\_II:\_A\_New\_Generation "Care Bears Movie II: A New Generation")_ (1986) and _[The Care Bears Adventure in Wonderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Care\_Bears\_Adventure\_in\_Wonderland "The Care Bears Adventure in Wonderland")_ (1987). Additional well-known popular-work based films include _[Bon Voyage, Charlie Brown (and Don't Come Back!!)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bon\_Voyage,\_Charlie\_Brown\_(and\_Don't\_Come\_Back!!) "Bon Voyage, Charlie Brown (and Don't Come Back!!)")_ (1980), _[Heavy Metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy\_Metal\_(film) "Heavy Metal (film)")_ (1981), _[The Adventures of Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Adventures\_of\_Mark\_Twain\_(1985\_film) "The Adventures of Mark Twain (1985 film)")_ (1985), _[The Secret of the Sword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Secret\_of\_the\_Sword "The Secret of the Sword")_ (1985), _[The Transformers: The Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Transformers:\_The\_Movie "The Transformers: The Movie")_ (1986), _[The Chipmunk Adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Chipmunk\_Adventure "The Chipmunk Adventure")_ (1987) and _[The BFG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_BFG\_(1989\_film) "The BFG (1989 film)")_ (1989); While other well-known original films include _[The King and the Mockingbird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_King\_and\_the\_Mockingbird "The King and the Mockingbird")_ (1980), _[American Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Pop "American Pop")_ (1981), _[The Last Unicorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Unicorn\_(film) "The Last Unicorn (film)")_ (1982), _[The Plague Dogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Plague\_Dogs\_(film) "The Plague Dogs (film)")_ (1982), _[Rock & Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock\_&\_Rule "Rock & Rule")_ (1983), _[Fire and Ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire\_and\_Ice\_(1983\_film) "Fire and Ice (1983 film)")_ (1983), _[Starchaser: The Legend of Orin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starchaser:\_The\_Legend\_of\_Orin "Starchaser: The Legend of Orin")_ (1985) and _[The Brave Little Toaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Brave\_Little\_Toaster "The Brave Little Toaster")_ (1987). The '80s also saw a resurgence of [Japanese anime films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime "Anime"): Inspired by the rarely successful release of his first film 1979's _[The Castle of Cagliostro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Castle\_of\_Cagliostro "The Castle of Cagliostro")_, [Hayao Miyazaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayao_Miyazaki "Hayao Miyazaki") went to produce _[Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausica%C3%A4\_of\_the\_Valley\_of\_the\_Wind\_(film) "Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (film)")_ (1984) for [Topcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topcraft "Topcraft"). The film's huge success convinced [Hayao Miyazaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayao_Miyazaki "Hayao Miyazaki") to form [Studio Ghibli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Ghibli "Studio Ghibli") which would then produce several critically acclaimed films of the decade including _[Castle in the Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle\_in\_the\_Sky "Castle in the Sky")_ (1986), _[My Neighbor Totoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Neighbor\_Totoro "My Neighbor Totoro")_ (1988), _[Grave of the Fireflies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grave\_of\_the\_Fireflies "Grave of the Fireflies")_ (1988) and _[Kiki's Delivery Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiki's\_Delivery\_Service "Kiki's Delivery Service")_ (1989). Other well-known anime films of that decade include _[Golgo 13: The Professional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golgo\_13:\_The\_Professional "Golgo 13: The Professional")_ (1983), _[Macross: Do You Remember Love?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macross:\_Do\_You\_Remember\_Love%3F "Macross: Do You Remember Love?")_ (1984), _[Lensman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lensman\_(1984\_film) "Lensman (1984 film)")_ (1984), _[Vampire Hunter D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vampire\_Hunter\_D\_(1985\_film) "Vampire Hunter D (1985 film)")_ (1985), _[Royal Space Force: The Wings of Honneamise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal\_Space\_Force:\_The\_Wings\_of\_Honneamise "Royal Space Force: The Wings of Honneamise")_ (1987), _[Akira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akira\_(1988\_film) "Akira (1988 film)")_ (1988) and _[Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Nemo:\_Adventures\_in\_Slumberland "Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland")_ (1989). Additionally, the first-ever theatrical animated franchise: [the Doraemon film series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Doraemon_films "List of Doraemon films") (based on the [anime and manga series of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doraemon "Doraemon")) began in 1980 with the release of _[Doraemon: Nobita's Dinosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doraemon:\_Nobita's\_Dinosaur "Doraemon: Nobita's Dinosaur")_ (1980).
*   _**[Blockbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster\_(entertainment) "Blockbuster (entertainment)")**_: The decade started by continuing the blockbuster boom of the mid-[1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970s_in_film "1970s in film"). The sequel to [1977's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_in_film "1977 in film")_[Star Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Wars\_(film) "Star Wars (film)")_, _[The Empire Strikes Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Empire\_Strikes\_Back "The Empire Strikes Back")_, opened in May [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_in_film "1980 in film") becoming the highest-grossing film of the year. It is considered among the greatest films of all time (being the highest rated 1980s film on [IMDb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMDb "IMDb")). It was followed by _[Return of the Jedi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_of\_the\_Jedi "Return of the Jedi")_ (1983) finishing the _[Star Wars original trilogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Wars\_original\_trilogy "Star Wars original trilogy")_. _[Superman II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman\_II "Superman II")_ was released in Europe and Australia in late 1980, but not distributed in the United States until June 1981. Though now seen as [campier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_(style) "Camp (style)") over the original [1978](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_in_film "1978 in film")_[Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman\_(1978\_film) "Superman (1978 film)")_, _Superman II_ was received with a positive reaction. From the success of _The Empire Strikes Back_, creator [George Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lucas "George Lucas") teamed up with director [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg") to create one of the most iconic characters in the [1981](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_in_film "1981 in film") film _[Raiders of the Lost Ark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raiders\_of\_the\_Lost\_Ark "Raiders of the Lost Ark")_ starring [Harrison Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_Ford "Harrison Ford"), who had also co-starred in _The Empire Strikes Back_. The story about an archaeologist and adventurer, [Indiana Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_(character) "Indiana Jones (character)") (Ford), hired by the U.S. government to go on a quest for the mystical lost [Ark of the Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark_of_the_Covenant "Ark of the Covenant"), created waves of interest in old 1930s style [cliffhanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliffhanger "Cliffhanger")[serials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_film "Serial film") as well as [treasure hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_hunting "Treasure hunting")[adventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_film "Adventure film") like 1984's _[Romancing the Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romancing\_the\_Stone "Romancing the Stone")_. It became the highest-grossing film of 1981, leading to sequels all in the top-10 films of the decade. In 1982, Spielberg directed his fairy-tale, sci-fi family blockbuster _[E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E.T.\_the\_Extra-Terrestrial "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial")_, which shattered all records, earning 40% more than any Star-Wars film, and double or triple the revenue of 46 of the top 50 films.
*   _**[Comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy\_film "Comedy film")**_: The [disaster films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_film "Disaster film") of the past decade were [spoofed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoof_film "Spoof film") in the gag comedy _[Airplane!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airplane! "Airplane!")_, paving the way for more of the same style of humor in such releases as _[Airplane II: The Sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airplane\_II:\_The\_Sequel "Airplane II: The Sequel")_ (1982), _[Top Secret!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top\_Secret! "Top Secret!")_ (1984) and _[The Naked Gun: From the Files of Police Squad!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Naked\_Gun:\_From\_the\_Files\_of\_Police\_Squad! "The Naked Gun: From the Files of Police Squad!")_ (1988). Popular comedy stars in the '80s included [Leslie Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Nielsen "Leslie Nielsen"), [John Candy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Candy "John Candy"), [Steve Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Martin "Steve Martin"), [Eddie Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Murphy "Eddie Murphy"), [Rick Moranis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Moranis "Rick Moranis"), [Bill Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Murray "Bill Murray"), [Chevy Chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevy_Chase "Chevy Chase") and [Dan Aykroyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Aykroyd "Dan Aykroyd"). Many had come to prominence on the NBC TV series _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_, including Bill Murray, Steve Martin and Chevy Chase. Eddie Murphy made a success of comedy-[action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film "Action film") films including _[48 Hrs.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48\_Hrs. "48 Hrs.")_ (1982) and the _[Beverly Hills Cop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly\_Hills\_Cop "Beverly Hills Cop")_ series (1984–1993). Also in the top-50 films were the romantic comedies _["Crocodile" Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%22Crocodile%22\_Dundee "\"Crocodile\" Dundee")_ (1986), _[Crocodile Dundee II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile\_Dundee\_II "Crocodile Dundee II")_ (1988) and _[Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur\_(1981\_film) "Arthur (1981 film)")_ (1981). Influenced largely by 1978's _[National Lampoon's Animal House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Lampoon's\_Animal\_House "National Lampoon's Animal House")_, the decade also saw the continued rise of [teen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_film "Teen film")[sex comedies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_comedies "Sex comedies") like _[Fast Times at Ridgemont High](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast\_Times\_at\_Ridgemont\_High "Fast Times at Ridgemont High")_, _[Porky's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porky's "Porky's")_ and _[Revenge of the Nerds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge\_of\_the\_Nerds "Revenge of the Nerds")_ (the later two of these had sequels). Also popular were the films of [John Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hughes_(filmmaker) "John Hughes (filmmaker)") such as _[Ferris Bueller's Day Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferris\_Bueller's\_Day\_Off "Ferris Bueller's Day Off")_ (1986). _[Heathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heathers "Heathers")_ (1988) provided a [tongue-in-cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue-in-cheek "Tongue-in-cheek") approach to the teenage comedy genre, showcasing the murders (disguised as suicides) of several popular students at a U.S. high school. Other notable comedies of the decade include the gender-swap film _[Tootsie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tootsie "Tootsie")_ (1982), _[Broadcast News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast\_News\_(film) "Broadcast News (film)")_ (1987), and a brief spate of age-reversal films including _[Big](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_(film) "Big (film)")_, _[18 Again!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18\_Again! "18 Again!")_, _[Vice Versa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice\_Versa\_(1988\_film) "Vice Versa (1988 film)")_ and _[Like Father, Like Son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like\_Father\_Like\_Son\_(1987\_film) "Like Father Like Son (1987 film)")_. Also notable were the _[Police Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Academy\_(film\_series) "Police Academy (film series)")_ series of broad comedies, produced between 1984 and 1993.
*   _**[Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance\_in\_film "Dance in film")**_: Many movies during the 1980s were centered around dancing and heavily influenced by [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV")[music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video"). _[Flashdance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashdance "Flashdance")_ (1983), _[Footloose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footloose "Footloose")_ (1984), and _[Dirty Dancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirty\_Dancing "Dirty Dancing")_ (1987) were all extremely successful as well as their soundtracks.
*   _**[Drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama\_(film\_and\_television) "Drama (film and television)")**_: Among the historical, romantic, and dramatic films, several were well received at the box office, including _[Rain Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain\_Man "Rain Man")_ (1988), _[On Golden Pond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_Golden\_Pond\_(1981\_film) "On Golden Pond (1981 film)")_ (1981), _[Terms of Endearment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terms\_of\_Endearment "Terms of Endearment")_ (1983), _[The Color Purple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Color\_Purple\_(1985\_film) "The Color Purple (1985 film)")_ (1985) and _[Out of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out\_of\_Africa\_(film) "Out of Africa (film)")_ (1985). Also notable in critical success were _[Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandhi\_(film) "Gandhi (film)")_ (1982), _[Sophie's Choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie's\_Choice\_(film) "Sophie's Choice (film)")_ (also 1982) and _[A Passage to India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Passage\_to\_India\_(film) "A Passage to India (film)")_ (1984). [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg")'s _[Always](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Always\_(1989\_film) "Always (1989 film)")_ was one of the two last Hollywood films to be released in the 1980s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-4)
*   _**[Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy\_film "Fantasy film")**_: Fantasies saw a resurgence particularly in [sword and sorcery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sword_and_sorcery "Sword and sorcery") films. In 1981, _[Dragonslayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragonslayer\_(1981\_film) "Dragonslayer (1981 film)")_ and _[Excalibur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur\_(film) "Excalibur (film)")_ started it off, but it was [1982's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_in_film "1982 in film")_[Conan the Barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_the\_Barbarian\_(1982\_film) "Conan the Barbarian (1982 film)")_ which caused the fantasy explosion. The epic starred [Arnold Schwarzenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger") in his acting breakthrough as he began his ascent to stardom. Loosely based on the original tales by [Robert E. Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Howard "Robert E. Howard"), the film was written by the unlikely pairing of [Oliver Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Stone "Oliver Stone") and [John Milius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Milius "John Milius"). Its sequel followed in [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_in_film "1984 in film") with the light-weight _[Conan the Destroyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan\_the\_Destroyer "Conan the Destroyer")_. Schwarzenegger returned again to a similar sword-wielding role in [1985's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_in_film "1985 in film")_[Red Sonja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Sonja\_(1985\_film) "Red Sonja (1985 film)")_. The same year as _Conan the Barbarian_, similar films followed such as _[The Sword and the Sorcerer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sword\_and\_the\_Sorcerer "The Sword and the Sorcerer")_, _[The Beastmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Beastmaster "The Beastmaster")_ and the _[Ator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ator "Ator")_ films. Fairy-tale fantasy was also popular with films such as _[The NeverEnding Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_NeverEnding\_Story\_(film) "The NeverEnding Story (film)")_ (1984), _[Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legend\_(1985\_film) "Legend (1985 film)")_ (1985) and _[The Princess Bride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Princess\_Bride "The Princess Bride")_ (1987). [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney "Disney")'s _[Return to Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_to\_Oz "Return to Oz")_, a big-budget sequel to 1939's classic _[The Wizard of Oz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wizard\_of\_Oz\_(1939\_film) "The Wizard of Oz (1939 film)")_, was a major flop, yet became a major success on home video. Jim Henson's _[Labyrinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labyrinth\_(1986\_film) "Labyrinth (1986 film)")_ (1986) was not an initial success but has since become a major cult classic. Hong Kong's _[A Chinese Ghost Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Chinese\_Ghost\_Story "A Chinese Ghost Story")_ (1987) blended fantasy with several other genres such as horror, action, comedy, and romance to great effect, becoming an international favorite all over Asia.
*   _**[Horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror\_film "Horror film")**_: Creativity from [1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970s_in_film "1970s in film") horror films extended throughout the 1980s, except having more gore, with many successful 1980s horror films having numerous sequels as their murderers were themselves unstoppable. [Stanley Kubrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick") directed his horror film _[The Shining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shining\_(film) "The Shining (film)")_ (1980). The creative and violent _[The Evil Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Evil\_Dead "The Evil Dead")_ (1981) with its secluded atmosphere is seen by many as one of the best in its genre, leading to its inevitable sequel _[Evil Dead II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evil\_Dead\_II "Evil Dead II")_ in [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_in_film "1987 in film"). _Halloween_ director [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter")'s _[The Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Thing\_(1982\_film) "The Thing (1982 film)")_ (1982) shocked audiences in its effects, as did [David Cronenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cronenberg "David Cronenberg")'s graphic and gory _[Scanners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanners "Scanners")_ (1981). Sequels to _[Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween\_(1978\_film) "Halloween (1978 film)")_ (1978), _[Friday the 13th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday\_the\_13th\_(1980\_film) "Friday the 13th (1980 film)")_ (1980), and _[A Nightmare on Elm Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Nightmare\_on\_Elm\_Street "A Nightmare on Elm Street")_ (1984) were the popular face of horror films in the 1980s, unkillable as their antagonists were, a trend reviled by most critics. [Dan O'Bannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_O'Bannon "Dan O'Bannon")'s _[The Return of the Living Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Return\_of\_the\_Living\_Dead "The Return of the Living Dead")_ and [Stuart Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Gordon "Stuart Gordon")'s _[Re-Animator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-Animator "Re-Animator")_ soon followed. In 1986, the [James Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cameron "James Cameron") film _[Aliens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliens\_(film) "Aliens (film)")_ was released a few weeks before [David Cronenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cronenberg "David Cronenberg")'s remake of _[The Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fly\_(1986\_film) "The Fly (1986 film)")_. Films such as _[Ghostbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostbusters "Ghostbusters")_, [Joe Dante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Dante "Joe Dante")'s _[Gremlins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremlins "Gremlins")_ (both 1984) and [Tim Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Burton "Tim Burton")'s _[Beetlejuice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beetlejuice "Beetlejuice")_ (1988) started a trend for horror comedies. _[Child's Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child's\_Play\_(1988\_film) "Child's Play (1988 film)")_ (1988) started the popular [killer doll franchise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child's_Play_(film_series) "Child's Play (film series)") starring [Brad Dourif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Dourif "Brad Dourif") as the infamous killer doll [Chucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chucky_(Child's_Play) "Chucky (Child's Play)").
*   _**[James Bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James\_Bond "James Bond")**_: The James Bond film series entered its third decade in 1981 with [Roger Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Moore "Roger Moore") starring in the more realistic _[For Your Eyes Only](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For\_Your\_Eyes\_Only\_(film) "For Your Eyes Only (film)")_ after the outlandish excess of _[Moonraker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonraker\_(film) "Moonraker (film)")_ in 1979. The decade saw the beginning of a new era for Bond since the previous decade's directors originally directed a [1960s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960s_in_film "1960s in film") Bond; the new director brought to the series, [John Glen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glen_(director) "John Glen (director)"), criticized for a less stylistic and more "workman" style of direction, directed all the [EON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EON_Productions "EON Productions") Bond films from 1981 to 1989. _Moonraker_ was the last for regular [Bernard Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lee "Bernard Lee") who portrayed Bond's boss [M](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M_(James_Bond) "M (James Bond)"). For the 1980s Bonds, a collection of numerous [MI6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MI6 "MI6") superiors would brief Bond on his missions. [1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_in_film "1983 in film") was a significant year for the series as a non-EON Bond was released, _[Never Say Never Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never\_Say\_Never\_Again "Never Say Never Again")_, directed by _The Empire Strikes Back_ director [Irvin Kershner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irvin_Kershner "Irvin Kershner"), with [Sean Connery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") returning to the role for the first time since 1971's _[Diamonds Are Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamonds\_Are\_Forever\_(film) "Diamonds Are Forever (film)")_; it was competing with the next EON film, _[Octopussy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octopussy "Octopussy")_ at the box office with media dubbing the situation "The Battle of the Bonds". Even lesser known in the same year was one-time Bond [George Lazenby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lazenby "George Lazenby") appearing in the TV reunion film _[The Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Return\_of\_the\_Man\_from\_U.N.C.L.E. "The Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.")_ as Bond-like character "JB". _[A View to a Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_View\_to\_a\_Kill "A View to a Kill")_ (1985) was the last for Roger Moore before [Timothy Dalton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Dalton "Timothy Dalton") was chosen as the new Bond in 1987's _[The Living Daylights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Living\_Daylights "The Living Daylights")_ and lastly in [1989's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_in_film "1989 in film")_[Licence to Kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licence\_to\_Kill "Licence to Kill")_.
*   _**[Martial Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial\_arts\_film "Martial arts film")**_: In Hong Kong, most action stars were either already skilled or at least partially trained in [kung fu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung_fu "Kung fu"). Many also worked as fight choreographers with backgrounds in [stage combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_combat "Stage combat") such as the comedic trio of [Jackie Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan "Jackie Chan"), [Sammo Hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammo_Hung "Sammo Hung"), and [Yuen Biao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Biao "Yuen Biao") (a.k.a. the Three Dragons) who were all part of [The Seven Little Fortunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seven_Little_Fortunes "The Seven Little Fortunes") troupe as children. Though the likes of [Jet Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Li "Jet Li") and [Yuen Woo-ping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Woo-ping "Yuen Woo-ping") were more known for being in front of or behind the camera respectively. Not to be left out, female action stars such as [Michelle Yeoh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Yeoh "Michelle Yeoh"), [Cynthia Rothrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Rothrock "Cynthia Rothrock"), [Yukari Oshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yukari_Oshima "Yukari Oshima"), [Moon Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_Lee_(Hong_Kong_actress) "Moon Lee (Hong Kong actress)"), and [Cynthia Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cynthia_Khan "Cynthia Khan") established the [girls with guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girls_with_guns "Girls with guns") trend during the latter half of the decade, which also heavily showcased [hand-to-hand combat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand-to-hand_combat "Hand-to-hand combat") sequences. Meanwhile, Hollywood found its footing in the martial arts subgenre with the likes of [Chuck Norris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Norris "Chuck Norris"), [Jean-Claude Van Damme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Claude_Van_Damme "Jean-Claude Van Damme"), and [Steven Seagal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Seagal "Steven Seagal"). All across-the-board, notable films include _[Shaolin Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaolin\_Temple\_(1982\_film) "Shaolin Temple (1982 film)")_, _[Zu Warriors from the Magic Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zu\_Warriors\_from\_the\_Magic\_Mountain "Zu Warriors from the Magic Mountain")_, _[Wheels on Meals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheels\_on\_Meals "Wheels on Meals")_, _[Big Trouble in Little China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Trouble\_in\_Little\_China "Big Trouble in Little China")_, _[Dragons Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragons\_Forever "Dragons Forever")_, _[Bloodsport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodsport\_(film) "Bloodsport (film)")_, and _[Miracles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miracles\_(1989\_film) "Miracles (1989 film)")_.
*   _**[Rite-of-Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rite\_of\_passage "Rite of passage")**_: Beyond just the teenager [coming-of-age stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming-of-age_stories "Coming-of-age stories"), more complex rite-of-passage films had older actors changing or transforming through the rituals. So although teenagers were the focus of 1983's _[Risky Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risky\_Business "Risky Business")_, 1984's _[The Karate Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Karate\_Kid\_(1984\_film) "The Karate Kid (1984 film)")_ and its sequels (1986, 1989), and 1985's _[The Breakfast Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Breakfast\_Club "The Breakfast Club")_ and _[St. Elmo's Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St.\_Elmo's\_Fire\_(film) "St. Elmo's Fire (film)")_ featuring the [Brat Pack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brat_Pack "Brat Pack"), older people with troubled lives were the subjects of _[Top Gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top\_Gun "Top Gun")_ (1986) or _[An Officer and a Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Officer\_and\_a\_Gentleman "An Officer and a Gentleman")_ in trying to become a fighter pilot, a female [welder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welder "Welder") in _[Flashdance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashdance "Flashdance")_ transforming into a [ballet dancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet_dancer "Ballet dancer"), and _[Cocoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocoon\_(film) "Cocoon (film)")'_ s (1985) elderly set overcoming old age. Even _[The Big Chill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_Chill\_(film) "The Big Chill (film)")_ (1983) reunion was a rite-of-passage that challenged old classmates to redirect their lives after the suicide of a friend. [The Goonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Goonies "The Goonies") in 1985 and [Stand by Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand_by_Me_(film) "Stand by Me (film)") in 1986 were both successful at the box office and went on to be considered classics of the decade. They also both featured a number young actors that would see future success both on the big screen and the small screen.
*   _**[Science Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_fiction\_film "Science fiction film")**_: Continuing the 1970s' sci-fi boom was Australian post-apocalyptic _[Mad Max 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_Max\_2 "Mad Max 2")_, with a leather-clad outlaw fighting road barbarians in the futuristic desert wasteland. Another futuristic adventure released the same year, _[Escape from New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape\_from\_New\_York "Escape from New York")_, also saw an [anti-hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-hero "Anti-hero") set in a [dystopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopian "Dystopian") future. In [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_in_film "1982 in film"), yet another film set in a dystopian future, the [Tech-noirish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tech-noir "Tech-noir")_[Blade Runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade\_Runner "Blade Runner")_ starred Harrison Ford as a detective searching for renegade androids. Sci-fi films aimed at younger audiences included the two _[Star Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Wars "Star Wars")_ films, _[The Empire Strikes Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Empire\_Strikes\_Back "The Empire Strikes Back")_ and _[Return of the Jedi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Return\_of\_the\_Jedi "Return of the Jedi")_, as well as the [_Back to the Future_ trilogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_the_Future_(franchise) "Back to the Future (franchise)") and [Steven Spielberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Spielberg "Steven Spielberg")'s _[E.T.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E.T.\_the\_Extra-Terrestrial "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial")_. The [Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Trek "Star Trek") series became a big screen success with four movies being released during the 1980s.
*   _**[Sequels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequels "Sequels")**_: In the late 1970s and early 1980s, a trend emerged toward the release of sequels based on recently successful productions. Among the sequels were _[Damien: Omen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damien:\_Omen\_II "Damien: Omen II")_, _[Revenge of the Pink Panther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenge\_of\_the\_Pink\_Panther "Revenge of the Pink Panther")_, _The Final Conflict_ (a.k.a. _[Omen III: The Final Conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omen\_III:\_The\_Final\_Conflict "Omen III: The Final Conflict")_), _[Grease 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grease\_2 "Grease 2")_, _[Trail of the Pink Panther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trail\_of\_the\_Pink\_Panther "Trail of the Pink Panther")_, _[The Great Muppet Caper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Great\_Muppet\_Caper "The Great Muppet Caper")_, _[Porky's II: The Next Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porky's\_II:\_The\_Next\_Day "Porky's II: The Next Day")_ and _[Porky's Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porky's\_Revenge "Porky's Revenge")_.
*   _**[Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_film "Sports film")**_: [Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") was especially popular on the big screen as evidenced by the releases of _[The Natural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Natural\_(film) "The Natural (film)")_, _[Bull Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bull\_Durham "Bull Durham")_, _[Major League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major\_League\_(film) "Major League (film)")_, and _[Field of Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field\_of\_Dreams "Field of Dreams")_. As well as [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing") with _[Raging Bull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raging\_Bull "Raging Bull")_, _[Rocky III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky\_III "Rocky III")_, and _[Rocky IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky\_IV "Rocky IV")_. Though other competitions were represented by the likes of _[Caddyshack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caddyshack "Caddyshack")_ ([golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf")), _[Chariots of Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chariots\_of\_Fire "Chariots of Fire")_ ([track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field#Track "Track and field")), _[The Color of Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Color\_of\_Money "The Color of Money")_ ([pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_(cue_sports) "Pool (cue sports)")), _[Hoosiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoosiers\_(film) "Hoosiers (film)")_ ([basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball")), and _[Over the Top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Over\_the\_Top\_(1987\_film) "Over the Top (1987 film)")_ ([arm wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm_wrestling "Arm wrestling")).
*   _**[Thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller\_film "Thriller film")**_: The 1980s saw an immense amount of thriller films, many being of an [erotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erotic_thriller "Erotic thriller") nature, including _[Body Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body\_Heat "Body Heat")_ (1981) and _[Fatal Attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatal\_Attraction "Fatal Attraction")_ (1987). Perhaps two of the most influential examples of 1980s thriller films were [David Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lynch "David Lynch")'s bizarre [cult classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_classic "Cult classic")_[Blue Velvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue\_Velvet\_(film) "Blue Velvet (film)")_ (1986), which dealt with the underworld of a seemingly idyllic U.S. suburbia, a subject which has spawned many imitations well into the first decade of the 21st century and [Stanley Kubrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kubrick "Stanley Kubrick")'s horror/thriller _[The Shining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shining\_(film) "The Shining (film)")_ (1980).
*   _**[Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western\_(genre) "Western (genre)")**_: A stylish form of western was evolving, with films such as _[Pale Rider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pale\_Rider "Pale Rider")_, _[Silverado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silverado\_(film) "Silverado (film)")_ (both 1985) and _[Young Guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young\_Guns\_(film) "Young Guns (film)")_ (1988).

## Content

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=1980s_in_film&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Content")]

The decade saw an increased amount of [nudity in film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nudity_in_film "Nudity in film"), as well as the increasing emphasis in the American industry on film franchises; especially in the [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction_film "Science fiction film"), [horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_film "Horror film"), and [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_films "Action films") genres. Much of the reliance on these effects-driven movies was due in part to the _[Star Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Wars "Star Wars")_ films at the advent of this decade and the new cinematic visuals they helped to pioneer.

With the release of 1984's _[Red Dawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Dawn "Red Dawn")_, the [PG-13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PG-13_(Motion_Picture_Association) "PG-13 (Motion Picture Association)") rating was introduced in the U.S. to accommodate films that straddled the line between PG and R. Which was mainly due to the controversies surrounding the violence of the PG films _[Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana\_Jones\_and\_the\_Temple\_of\_Doom "Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom")_ and _[Gremlins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremlins "Gremlins")_ from earlier that same year.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-5)

Some have considered the 1980s in retrospect as one of the weaker decades for American cinema in terms of the qualities of the films released. Filmmaker [Quentin Tarantino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino") has voiced his own view that the 1980s was one of the worst eras for American films.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-6) Film critic Kent Jones also shares this opinion.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-7) However, film theorist [David Bordwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bordwell "David Bordwell") countered this notion, saying that the "megapicture mentality" was already existent in the 1970s, which is evident in the ten highest-grossing films of that decade, as well as with how many of the filmmakers part of New Hollywood were still able to direct many great pictures in the 1980s ([Martin Scorsese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese"), [Brian de Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_de_Palma "Brian de Palma"), [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter "John Carpenter"), etc.).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_film#cite_note-8)

_**Nineteen Eighty-Four**_ (stylized as _**1984**_) is a 1984 British [dystopian film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopian_film "Dystopian film") written and directed by Michael Radford, based on [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s [1949 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four"). Starring [John Hurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hurt "John Hurt"), [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton"), [Suzanna Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanna_Hamilton "Suzanna Hamilton") and [Cyril Cusack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Cusack "Cyril Cusack"), it follows the life of [Winston Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Smith_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Winston Smith (Nineteen Eighty-Four)") (Hurt), a low-ranking civil servant in a war-torn London in [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Oceania (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a [totalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarian "Totalitarian") superstate ruled by [Ingsoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingsoc "Ingsoc") and its leader [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-7) Smith struggles to maintain his sanity and his grip on reality as the regime's overwhelming power and influence persecute [individualism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individualism "Individualism") and individual thinking on both a political and a personal level.

_Nineteen Eighty-Four_ was Burton's last screen appearance; it was released two months after his death and is dedicated to him.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-tcmnotes-8) It was released in the United Kingdom on 10 October 1984 by [Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films"). It received positive reviews from critics, with many highlighted Deakins' cinematography and use of [bleach bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_bypass "Bleach bypass"). It was nominated for a [BAFTA Award for Best Art Direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Art_Direction "BAFTA Award for Best Art Direction"), and won two [Evening Standard British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards") for Best Film and Best Actor.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

In a dystopian 1984, Winston Smith endures a squalid existence in the [totalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totalitarian "Totalitarian") superstate of [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_geography_of_Nineteen_Eighty-Four#Oceania "Political geography of Nineteen Eighty-Four") under the constant surveillance of the [Thought Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_Police "Thought Police"). He resides in London, the capital city of the territory of [Airstrip One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airstrip_One "Airstrip One"), formerly Britain, and works in a small office cubicle at the [Ministry of Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Truth "Ministry of Truth"), rewriting history as dictated by [the Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingsoc "Ingsoc") and its supreme leader, [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), who never appears publicly but instead appears only on propaganda posters, advertising billboards and television monitors. Smith attends mandatory public rallies at Victory Square (formerly [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square")), where citizens are shown propaganda films of the current war situation as well as contradictory and false news stories about Oceania's war effort to unite the civilized world under Big Brother's rule. While his co-worker and neighbour Parsons seems content to follow the state's laws, Winston, haunted by painful childhood memories and restless carnal desires, keeps a secret diary of his private thoughts, thus creating evidence of his [thoughtcrime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoughtcrime "Thoughtcrime"). However, he tries to do it out of sight of the telescreens, to maintain his safety.

His life greatly changes when he is accosted by his fellow Outer Party worker [Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Julia (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a mysterious, bold-looking, sensual and free-spirited young woman who works as a print machine mechanic in the Ministry of Truth, and they begin an illicit affair. During their first meeting in the remote countryside, they exchange subversive ideas before having sex. Shortly after, Winston rents a room above a pawn shop in the less restrictive proletarian area where they continue their liaison. Julia procures [contraband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contraband "Contraband") food and clothing on the black market, and for a brief few months they secretly meet and enjoy an idyllic life of relative freedom and contentment together.

Their affair comes to an end one evening, when the Thought Police suddenly raid the flat and arrest them both. It is later revealed that a [telescreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telescreen "Telescreen") hidden behind a picture on the wall in their room recorded their transgressions and that the elderly proprietor of the pawn shop, Mr. Charrington, is a covert agent of the Thought Police. Winston and Julia are taken away to the [Ministry of Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Love "Ministry of Love") to be detained, questioned and "rehabilitated" separately. There [O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Brien_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "O'Brien (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), a high-ranking member of the Inner Party whom Winston had believed to be a fellow thoughtcriminal and agent of the resistance movement led by the Party's archenemy, [Emmanuel Goldstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Goldstein "Emmanuel Goldstein"), systematically tortures him.

O'Brien instructs Winston about the state's true purpose and schools him in a kind of [catechism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechism "Catechism") on the principles of _[doublethink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doublethink "Doublethink")_–the practice of holding two contradictory thoughts in the mind simultaneously. For his final rehabilitation, Winston is brought to [Room 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Room_101 "Room 101"), where O'Brien tells him he will be subjected to the "worst thing in the world", designed specifically around Smith's personal phobias. When confronted with this unbearable horror–a cage filled with wild rats–Winston's psychological resistance finally and irretrievably breaks down; he hysterically repudiates his allegiance to Julia. Seemingly subjugated and purged of any rebellious thoughts, impulses or personal attachments, Winston is restored to physical health and released.

Winston returns to the Chestnut Tree Café, where he had seen the rehabilitated thoughtcriminals Jones, Aaronson and Rutherford (themselves once prominent but later disgraced members of the Inner Party) who have since been "vaporized" and rendered [unpersons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspeak#Newspeak_vocabulary "Newspeak"). While sitting at the chess table, Winston is approached by Julia, who was similarly "rehabilitated". They share a bottle of Victory Gin and impassively exchange a few words about how they have betrayed each other. In spite of everything they have gone through, they still reaffirm their bond and express desire to see each other again. After she leaves, Winston watches a broadcast of himself on the large telescreen humbly and remorsefully confessing his "crimes" against the state and imploring forgiveness from the populace.

Upon hearing a news report declaring the Oceanian army's utter rout of [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_geography_of_Nineteen_Eighty-Four#Eurasia_and_Eastasia "Political geography of Nineteen Eighty-Four")'s forces in North Africa, Winston, appearing to have been deprived of his freedom to think and feel for himself and reduced to a mere shell of a man, soon to be deprived of his physical existence, looks at the still image of Big Brother that appears on the telescreen but then quickly turns away from it and looks in the direction of Julia with tears in his eyes as the words "I love you" are heard whispered in his voice.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Production")]

In the winter of 1983 the director Michael Radford asked his producer to try to obtain the rights to Orwell's novel, with low expectations that they were available. It turned out that the rights were held by Marvin Rosenblum, a lawyer in Chicago who had been trying on his own to get such a film produced.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) Rosenblum agreed to become an executive producer, and while the producer Simon Perry raised the production money from [Richard Branson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Branson "Richard Branson"), Radford wrote the script, inspired by his idea to make a "science fiction film made in 1948".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) The script was finished in three weeks.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)

For the role of [O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O'Brien_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "O'Brien (Nineteen Eighty-Four)"), [Paul Scofield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Scofield "Paul Scofield") was originally contracted to play the part, but had to withdraw after sustaining a broken leg while filming _[The Shooting Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shooting\_Party "The Shooting Party")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-10)[Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins "Anthony Hopkins"), [Sean Connery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Connery "Sean Connery") and [Rod Steiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Steiger "Rod Steiger") were all then considered.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) Richard Burton, who was living in [Haiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti "Haiti"), joined the production six weeks into its shooting schedule[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9) and insisted on his costume of a [boiler suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boiler_suit "Boiler suit") being hand-made for him in [Savile Row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savile_Row "Savile Row").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-12)

Some sources claim that [principal photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began on 19 March 1984, ending later the same year in October 1984.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-tcmnotes-8) It was released that same month, however, and a title card at the end explicitly states that it "was photographed in and around London during the period April–June 1984, the exact time and setting imagined by Orwell."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-13) The budget was originally £2.5 million, but this rose during filming and additional funds were required.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-14) The opening scenes showing the [Two Minutes Hate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_Minutes_Hate "Two Minutes Hate") were filmed in a grass-covered hangar at [RAF Hullavington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Hullavington "RAF Hullavington") near [Chippenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chippenham "Chippenham") in Wiltshire.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-15) Some scenes set in Victory Square were also filmed at [Alexandra Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Palace "Alexandra Palace") in London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-16)[Senate House (University of London)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_House_(University_of_London) "Senate House (University of London)") was used for exterior shots of the [Ministry of Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Truth "Ministry of Truth").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The disused [Battersea Power Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battersea_Power_Station "Battersea Power Station") in [Wandsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Wandsworth "London Borough of Wandsworth") served as the façade for the Victory Mansions, and the [Beckton Gas Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beckton_Gas_Works "Beckton Gas Works") in the [Docklands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Docklands "London Docklands") of [Newham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Borough_of_Newham "London Borough of Newham") was used as the setting for the proletarian zones. The pawnshop exterior, a pub scene and a scene with a prostitute were filmed in [Cheshire Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_Street "Cheshire Street") in the [East End of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_End_of_London "East End of London"), an area Orwell had visited and commented on in his first book, _[Down and Out in Paris and London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_and\_Out\_in\_Paris\_and\_London "Down and Out in Paris and London")_. The canteen interiors were filmed in a [disused grain mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Mills "Millennium Mills") at [Silvertown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silvertown "Silvertown"). In contrast, the idyllic, dreamlike "Golden Country", where Winston and Julia repair for their first tryst and which recurs in Winston's fantasies, was filmed in the southwest county of [Wiltshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiltshire "Wiltshire") at a natural circle of hills called "Roundway", near the town of [Devizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devizes "Devizes"). The scenes on the train were shot on the [Kent and East Sussex Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent_and_East_Sussex_Railway "Kent and East Sussex Railway"). The film shared a number of locations with [Terry Gilliam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Gilliam "Terry Gilliam")'s _[Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil\_(1985\_film) "Brazil (1985 film)")_, which was filmed the same year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-DenGeek-9)

Radford and the cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins") originally wanted to shoot the film in black and white, but the financial backers of the production, [Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films"), opposed this idea. Instead, Deakins used a film [processing technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_processing "Film processing") called [bleach bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach_bypass "Bleach bypass") to give a distinctive washed-out look to the film's color values. This technique was invented by the Japanese cinematographer [Kazuo Miyagawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuo_Miyagawa "Kazuo Miyagawa") for [Kon Ichikawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kon_Ichikawa "Kon Ichikawa")'s film _[Her Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her\_Brother "Her Brother")_ (1960), in imitation of a more complicated process developed by Technicolor and Deluxe for the [1956 version of _Moby Dick_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moby_Dick_(1956_film) "Moby Dick (1956 film)")_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film)#cite\_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen\_Eighty-Four\_(1984\_film)#cite\_note-18)_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-19) The process was recreated for this production by Key. The film is a very rare example of the technique being applied to every release print, rather than the [interpositive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpositive "Interpositive"), that was struck from the [original camera negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Original_camera_negative "Original camera negative"), or the internegative (struck from the interpositive); as the silver is retained in the print and cannot be reclaimed by the lab, the cost is higher, but the retained silver gives a "depth" to the projected image.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Release and reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Release and reception")]

_Nineteen Eighty-Four_ made its theatrical debut on 10 October in London and on 14 December in New York City.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-auto-20) It was released in the United States for one week in December 1984 at the [Egyptian Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grauman's_Egyptian_Theatre "Grauman's Egyptian Theatre") in Los Angeles to qualify for the [1985 Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/57th_Academy_Awards "57th Academy Awards") and grossed a house record of US$62,121, despite stormy weather.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-hv-21)

[Vincent Canby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Canby "Vincent Canby") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ said the film was "admirable, bleakly beautiful", although "not an easy film to watch".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-canby-3)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") awarded it 3.5/4 stars, writing that it "penetrates much more deeply into the novel's heart of darkness" than previous adaptations, and describing Hurt as "the perfect Winston Smith".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-22)

The [review aggregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") has given it a 76% approval rating, based on 33 reviews, with an average rating of 6.8/10. The site's critical consensus states:

> _1984_ doesn't fully emerge from the shadow of its source material, but still proves a solid, suitably discomfiting adaptation of a classic dystopian tale.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-23)

_Filmink_ called it "brilliant, incredible to look at, and emotionally devastating."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-al-24)

The review aggregation website [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic") has given it a rating of 67 out of 100 based on 8 critics, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-25)

## Score controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Score controversy")]

[![Image 5: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **needs [more citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Please help [improve this section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film) "Special:EditPage/Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984 film)") by [adding citations to reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Referencing_for_beginners "Help:Referencing for beginners"). Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(February 2017)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

[Virgin Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Films "Virgin Films") (formerly part of the [Virgin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Group "Virgin Group")), who financed the film, commissioned the British rock/pop duo [Eurythmics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurythmics "Eurythmics") to produce the music for the soundtrack after initially approaching [David Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bowie "David Bowie"), who demanded a fee that Virgin deemed to be too high.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-26) Radford objected to Virgin's insistence on using the more pop-oriented [electronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") Eurythmics music, as the traditional [orchestral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral "Orchestral")[score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_score "Film score") originally intended for the film had been composed entirely by [Dominic Muldowney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Muldowney "Dominic Muldowney") a few months earlier.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-al-24)

Against Radford's wishes, Virgin exercised their right of final cut and replaced Muldowney's musical [cues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cue_(theatrical) "Cue (theatrical)") with the new Eurythmics contributions. One Eurythmics song, "[Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_(Eurythmics_song) "Julia (Eurythmics song)")", was also heard in its entirety during the film's closing credits. However, Muldowney's main theme music (particularly the state anthem, "Oceania, 'tis for thee") was still prominently used in the film.

In November 1984 Virgin Records released the Eurythmics soundtrack album, containing considerably altered versions of their music heard in the film, under the title _[1984 (For the Love of Big Brother)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984\_(For\_the\_Love\_of\_Big\_Brother) "1984 (For the Love of Big Brother)")_. The album reached number 23 on the UK Album Chart, and was later certified Gold by the [BPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Phonographic_Industry "British Phonographic Industry") for sales in excess of 100,000 copies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-BPI-27) A song from the album, "[Sexcrime (Nineteen Eighty-Four)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexcrime_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four)_(Eurythmics_song) "Sexcrime (Nineteen Eighty-Four) (Eurythmics song)")", was released as a single just prior to the album and became one of Eurythmics' biggest hits, peaking at number 4 and was awarded a Silver disc for sales in excess of 250,000 copies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-BPI-27) The music video for the single made use of clips from the film. The track "Julia" was also released as a single which peaked just outside the Top 40.

Radford disowned Virgin's edit of the film containing the predominantly Eurythmics score and, during his acceptance speech at the [_Evening Standard_ British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards"), expressed his displeasure at Virgin's "foisting" the Eurythmics music on his film.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-auto-20) Radford withdrew the film from consideration at the [BAFTA awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA "BAFTA") in protest of Virgin's decision to change the musical score. Eurythmics responded with a statement of their own claiming no knowledge of prior agreements between Virgin and Radford/Muldowney and that they had accepted the offer to compose music for the film in good faith.

In 1999 Muldowney's complete orchestral score (24 tracks in total) was released on a special limited edition CD album under the title _Nineteen Eighty-Four: The Music of Oceania_, to commemorate the film's 15th anniversary. The CD booklet featured previously unseen production photographs and artwork as well as liner notes by Radford.

As of today, [Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer "Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer") owns the film's rights worldwide since they own both the Atlantic Releasing Corporation and the Virgin Films catalogues, and on their DVD release in North America in 2003, the film's colour is restored to a normal level of saturation and the Eurythmics contributions to the score were removed entirely and replaced with Muldowney's musical cues as Radford had originally intended—although both Eurythmics and Muldowney are still jointly credited in the opening and closing titles. This DVD release was quickly discontinued and currently remains out of print. This version had previously been shown by [Channel 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_4 "Channel 4") in the UK in the late 1980s. However, while the MGM DVD release of the film in the UK in 2004 features the desaturated visuals, it has the mixed Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtrack on the English- and French-language audio tracks, but the purely Muldowney soundtrack on the German- and Spanish-language audio tracks.

In 2013 the film was re-released on DVD in North America by TGG Direct on a double feature with _[Megaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megaville "Megaville")_ (1990), under licence from MGM. This DVD release also features the original mix of Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtracks, as well as the theatrical desaturated colour palette. In 2015 the film was released on Blu-ray in North America by Twilight Time in a limited 3,000 copy run, again, licensed by MGM. This release features the Eurythmics/Muldowney Soundtrack on one audio channel and Muldowney's orchestral score on another, as well as keeping true to the original colour scheme.

The version of the film which has been released on [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") services is the 2015 HD edition. It is available only with the original Eurythmics/Muldowney soundtrack.

The 2019 [Criterion Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criterion_Collection "Criterion Collection") release of the film features the original colour scheme (with a transfer supervised by the cinematographer [Roger Deakins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Deakins "Roger Deakins")) and includes both the Eurythmics soundtrack and the original score composed by Dominic Muldowney.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-28)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

It won the Best British Film of the Year award at the [Evening Standard British Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evening_Standard_British_Film_Awards "Evening Standard British Film Awards"). It also won The [Golden Tulip Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Tulip_Award "Golden Tulip Award") at the 1985 [Istanbul International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_International_Film_Festival "Istanbul International Film Festival").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Home media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Home media")]

[International Video Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Video_Entertainment "International Video Entertainment") paid US$2 million for North American [home video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_video "Home video") rights, the fifth-biggest deal ever at the time.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four_(1984_film)#cite_note-hv-21) Their initial VHS & Betamax releases came out in 1985, with a later release in 1989. [Avid Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avid_Home_Entertainment "Avid Home Entertainment") released it on VHS in 1990 and again in 1994. In between the Avid releases, [GoodTimes Home Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GoodTimes_Home_Video "GoodTimes Home Video") released a VHS in LP mode in 1992. After acquiring ITC Entertainment Group, [PolyGram Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PolyGram_Video "PolyGram Video") released their VHS in conjunction with [Sundance Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundance_Channel_(United_States) "Sundance Channel (United States)") in 1996.

In 2003 [MGM Home Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MGM_Home_Entertainment "MGM Home Entertainment") released it on DVD in North America and in the UK a year later; the American DVD only contains Muldowney's score while the UK DVD contains the mix of his and Eurythmics' soundtrack. TGG Direct re-released it on DVD in 2013 as a double feature with Megaville. It has been released on Blu-ray twice, first by [Twilight Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_Time_(home_video_label) "Twilight Time (home video label)") in 2015 as a limited 3,000-copy run and by [The Criterion Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Criterion_Collection "The Criterion Collection") in 2019. Both of these editions contain both the original theatrical Eurythmics score and the alternate Muldowney score.

In 2024 it was released on 4K [Blu-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blu-ray "Blu-ray") in Germany and Hungary.
